analysis.one_liner: Creates a federal commission to regulate large tech platforms on competition, privacy, and national security.
analysis.headline: The Warren-Graham bill to create a digital platform regulator was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee and died there without a hearing, markup, or vote before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would create a new independent federal agency, the Digital Consumer Protection Commission, with power over the biggest tech platforms. It would require dominant platforms to get federal licenses, ban them from favoring their own products, force them to separate businesses that conflict with their sellers, and presumptively block their future acquisitions unless proven to serve the public interest. It would also give users enforceable privacy rights and appeal rights over content moderation, ban noncompete, no-poach, forced-arbitration, and class-action-waiver agreements imposed by dominant platforms, and fine violators up to 15 percent of their parent company's annual revenue.
analysis.who_benefits: Users of large platforms would gain enforceable privacy rights (access, correction, deletion, limits on targeted advertising) and appeal rights over content moderation. Small businesses selling on platforms would gain from bans on self-preferencing and conflicts of interest, with divestiture as the remedy. Workers at dominant platforms would gain bans on noncompete, no-poach, predispute arbitration, and class-action waiver agreements. Consumers and startups would gain from new acquisition limits and interoperability requirements, backed by penalties up to 15 percent of parent-company annual revenue, officer liability, and state and private enforcement.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Platform users, small sellers, and platform workers

how_it_helps.text: Establishes an independent five-member Digital Consumer Protection Commission with jurisdiction over all covered entities and platform operators, authority to investigate, subpoena, write rules, and enforce.

Gives users privacy duties enforceable against platforms — duty of loyalty, care, mitigation, and confidentiality — plus rights to access, correct, port, and delete their data and limits on targeted advertising.

Bars dominant platforms from self-preferencing, tying, undue discrimination, and maintaining conflicts of interest between the platform and businesses that compete on it, with divestiture as the remedy — targeting the model in which a marketplace owner also sells its own products on that marketplace.

Presumptively prohibits dominant platforms from making future acquisitions unless the parties prove by clear and convincing evidence the deal serves the public interest, and allows the Commission to unwind past acquisitions that materially harmed it.

Bans noncompete agreements, no-poach agreements, predispute arbitration agreements, and predispute class-action waivers imposed by dominant platforms on users, trading partners, and employees — provisions that would put real bargaining power back with workers and small businesses dealing with the largest platforms.

Requires dominant platforms to disclose content-moderation criteria, notify users within 24 hours of restricting their content, and provide a real appeals process, with complaints going to the new Commission.

Backs it all with civil penalties up to 15 percent of a violator's ultimate parent entity's annual revenue, personal liability for the CEO, CFO, or chief security officer, federal contract debarment of 3 to 7 years, and enforcement by states and private parties.
Requires data portability and interoperability so users can leave a dominant platform and take their data with them, and imposes rules on data brokers.

analysis.who_pays: Large technology companies would bear licensing requirements, compliance and reporting costs, potential forced divestitures of conflicting lines of business, restrictions on acquisitions, and fines up to 15 percent of their parent company's annual revenue. Some of those costs would likely be passed through to advertisers and users, and the targeted-advertising and data-broker industries would lose a legal business model the bill curtails.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large tech platforms and data brokers

drawbacks.text: The bill's strongest worker protections — bans on noncompetes, no-poach deals, and forced arbitration — apply only to dominant platforms, leaving workers at every other large employer without them.

The licensing regime would require operators of dominant platforms to obtain and keep a federal license, and the content-moderation notice, reporting, and appeal mandates give a new agency broad power over how speech platforms operate — a design critics warned risks government overreach into online speech and heavy compliance costs.

The dominance thresholds (roughly 50 million U.S. users, $550 billion in parent sales or market value, or 1 billion worldwide users) draw bright lines that could incentivize companies to stay just under them, and although intentional avoidance is unlawful, enforcing that line would be contentious.

The bill covers only platform-related conduct; broad privacy and arbitration problems in the wider economy — the bill's 'covered entity' provisions notwithstanding — would still require separate legislation, so its consumer gains, while real, are scoped to the largest players.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer, small-seller, and worker benefits would have been substantial and directly aimed at the handful of companies with the most power over online commerce and speech, and the enforcement teeth (revenue-based penalties, officer liability, divestiture) were stronger than existing law. The honest costs are also real: a licensing scheme over speech platforms concentrates enormous discretion in a new commission, the content-moderation mandates would entangle government in moderation policy, and compliance costs at that scale are usually passed on. The bill's narrow scope — its labor protections reach only dominant-platform workers — blunts its headline ambitions. On balance it was a serious, well-aimed check on concentrated platform power with identifiable design risks, and it never got a hearing to work those risks out.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote until the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Elizabeth Warren introduced the bill on July 27, 2023, with Republican Senator Lindsey Graham as its cosponsor — an unusual bipartisan pairing on tech regulation.
That same day the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary.
The committee took no further action of any kind — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill never reached the Senate floor before the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
Because it never advanced, the commission, licensing regime, privacy duties, platform-conflict divestitures, acquisition limits, and worker protections it contained never took effect.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large digital platforms are better off: no new regulator, no licensing, no forced divestitures, no acquisition limits, and no revenue-based penalties. Thebill's two sponsors and the users and workers it would have protected gained nothing.

for.name: Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to create a Digital Consumer Protection Commission with licensing, antitrust, privacy, and national-security authority over dominant platforms.

for.name: Lindsay Graham
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, making it a bipartisan Warren-Graham pairing and the bill's only listed cosponsor.

against.name: Dick Durbin
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on July 27, 2023 and never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; it died in committee with no action listed after the referral.

against.name: Major technology platforms and their trade associations
against.what_they_did: Opposed legislation to regulate dominant platforms, including antitrust and privacy measures, through extensive lobbying during the 118th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had one Democratic sponsor and one Republican cosponsor, but with just two senators behind it and no committee or floor votes ever taken, no partisan split was ever measured.

industries.industry: Big tech platforms (search, social media, e-commerce, app stores)
industries.note: Platforms meeting the dominance thresholds would need a federal license, could be forced to divest businesses that conflict with their own sellers, would presumptively be blocked from future acquisitions, and could face fines up to 15 percent of parent-company annual revenue plus officer liability. This is the bill's central target: companies whose gatekeeping power over online commerce and speech is the source of the consumer harms the bill addresses.

The bill names data brokers for specific rules and subjects all covered entities to privacy duties, data-security requirements, and breach penalties, threatening a business built on trading personal data.

The bill imposes limitations on targeted advertising and defines the broad sensitive-data categories (location, biometrics, browsing) on which the ad-tech economy runs, directly shrinking the data available for ad targeting.
